title: Gig work: flexibility or just no rights?

turns.speaker: Holly
turns.text: The tribunal ruled they're workers, not contractors. Holiday pay, minimum wage, the lot.

turns.speaker: Aziz
turns.text: My cousin drives for them and he's genuinely not pleased about it. He likes picking his hours.

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: Those two things were never actually in tension, though. That's the framing the companies built and everyone accepted.

turns.speaker: Holly
turns.text: Meaning you can have flexible hours and holiday pay.

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: Plenty of countries do exactly that. The law just never had a category for it, so it got forced into one of two boxes.

turns.speaker: Aziz
turns.text: The thing he'd say is that the algorithm decides what he's offered, when, and at what price, and he can't negotiate any of it.

turns.speaker: Holly
turns.text: Which is the definition of not being your own boss.

turns.speaker: Holly
turns.text: A contractor sets a rate. He gets shown one.

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: And the earnings figures the platforms quote are before fuel, insurance, the vehicle and the waiting time.

turns.speaker: Aziz
turns.text: The waiting is the part people miss. Logged on, available, not being paid.

turns.speaker: Holly
turns.text: Which is why the ruling counts time from logging on rather than from accepting a job.

turns.speaker: Nour
turns.text: The risk is they respond by cutting the fleet and only keeping the busiest people.

turns.speaker: Aziz
turns.text: Which is what happened in Spain, more or less. Fewer riders, better paid, and the ones who left were furious.

points: A tribunal reclassified platform drivers as workers, granting holiday pay and minimum wage.
Some drivers object, valuing flexible hours.
Nour argues flexibility and employment rights were never genuinely in conflict, and other countries combine them.
Holly argues the algorithm setting prices and offers means drivers are not independent contractors, who would set their own rates.
Quoted earnings exclude fuel, insurance, vehicle costs and unpaid waiting time, which the ruling addresses by counting time from logging on.
They note the likely response is a smaller, better-paid fleet, as happened in Spain, which displaced riders resented.
